title: Tazria: the priest must look (Leviticus 13:2–3)
hookLine: the priest examines in person, never from a distance

cards: A rumor reaches you: so-and-so has really changed, and not for the better. You haven't seen them in a year. You've heard it from two people, maybe three, and by dinner it's easy to half believe it.
Leviticus thirteen imagines a camp where a mark appears on someone's skin. Everyone can see it. Neighbors could whisper; family could guess.
But the text gives the call to exactly one person, and it gives that person one instruction before anything else.

teach.b: Start with where the person goes.

When someone has a rising, a scab or a bright spot on the skin, they are brought to Aaron the priest or one of his sons. Not to the neighbors, not to the group, but to someone whose job is to look carefully.
Then the priest looks. The Hebrew verb ra'ah, to see, comes again and again in this chapter. Has the hair in the spot turned white?
Does it seem deeper than the skin? Only after looking does he say a word. No ruling from across the camp, no verdict by report.

teach.h: NOT AT DUSK, NOT ON A CLOUDY DAY.
teach.b: The Mishnah says the priest doesn't examine in the early morning or the evening, or indoors, or on a cloudy day, because in poor light a dull spot can look bright; and not at noon, when a bright one can look dull.
Even good eyes need good light.

And nobody judges their own. The Mishnah also says a person may examine anyone's affliction except his own, and one opinion adds: or a close relative's. People are bad judges of what's too close to them.
Put together, it's a whole ethic of looking: come close, look yourself, wait for the right light, and step aside when you can't see straight.
Some teachers carry it far beyond skin, to every time someone is tempted to decide about a person from a distance.

how: Jewish teaching on judging others draws on Pirkei Avot's advice to judge every person favorably and not to judge another until you stand in their place, and some teachers pair Tazria with it.

o: the priest's look: the exam of a skin mark
when a woman conceives: the portion's name
a bright spot: a mark that rises on skin

games.q: what's inside the looking — tap the pairs.

s: the priest could rule on a mark from across the camp
the text has him look at it himself before saying a word.
the Mishnah forbids examining on a cloudy day
in poor light a dull spot can look bright.
a person may examine their own affliction
the Mishnah says anyone's except your own.

games.q: you're the priest. it's dusk, the light is fading, and someone is brought to you with a mark on their skin. what do you do?
o: wait for good light to look.
ask the neighbors what they think.
games.why: the Mishnah says not in the early morning or evening, not indoors, not on a cloudy day. even the expert waits for good light.

practice: Think of someone you've formed an opinion about from a distance: from a story, a post, a single bad moment.
Ask yourself the priest's questions: have I actually seen this, or only heard it; am I looking in good light, or when I'm tired and annoyed; am I too close to judge fairly?
Then hold your opinion a little more loosely, until you can look again.

wordCard.voice: Tazria. The portion where the priest must come close and look for himself, in good light, before he says anything at all.

orig.note: Hebrew: "and the priest shall look": the phrase that comes again and again in Leviticus 13.

carryVoice: Your line: look, don't assume. Good light and a close look come before any verdict. That's day three hundred ninety-seven.
